title: Diogenes and the king
hook: Alexander offers him anything, and the Cynic asks him to stand out of his sunlight

segments.voice: Yesterday, Seneca's last hours, and the one gift he had left. Your line was the image of a life. What line did you write? Day thirty-four.
screen: `SENECA'S LAST HOURS — THE IMAGE OF A LIFE.`

segments.voice: After three heavy days, a lighter one, and one of the most famous encounters in the ancient world. Corinth, Greece, around 336 BCE. Alexander, the young king of Macedon, about twenty years old, already on his way to conquering most of the known world, comes to town. Everyone important rushes to congratulate him. One man doesn't come. So Alexander goes to find him. He's lying on the ground in the sun, an old man with a stick and a cloak and almost nothing else. The most powerful young man on earth stands over the man who owns nothing, and makes him an offer.
screen: `CORINTH, AROUND 336 BCE.` → `EVERYONE RUSHES TO THE KING.` → `ONE MAN STAYS IN THE SUN.`

segments.voice: The man was Diogenes of Sinope, the most famous Cynic of all. Remember the Cynics, from Zeno's story? The dog-like philosophers who owned nothing and said what they thought. Crates, the door-opener, was Diogenes's student. And a quick note: our source is a different Diogenes, Diogenes Laërtius, the biographer, writing centuries later. Same name, no relation. Here's the scene as he tells it. Alexander stands over the old man and says: ask me for anything you want. And Diogenes, squinting up, says: stand out of my light. That's it. The king had offered him the world, and what he wanted was the sun back. Diogenes lived like that on purpose. The stories say he slept in a big clay storage jar, walked around in broad daylight with a lamp, saying he was looking for a human being, and, asked where he was from, answered: I'm a citizen of the world. He wasn't always pleasant. The stories about him are full of rudeness and stunts, and plenty of Athenians found him unbearable. But the point underneath the stunts was serious. Almost everything people chase, he thought, is a kind of shade: it blocks the simple good that's already shining on you. And the story has a strange ending. Plutarch says that as Alexander walked away, with his officers laughing at the old man, the king said: if I weren't Alexander, I would be Diogenes. Maybe the king saw what the Cynic had. The one thing an empire couldn't give him, because he already had it: the light.
screen: `DIOGENES OF SINOPE, THE CYNIC.` · `ASK ME FOR ANYTHING.` · `A LAMP IN BROAD DAYLIGHT.` · `IF I WEREN'T ALEXANDER.` · then, large: `STAND OUT OF MY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If there's sunlight near you, go and sit or stand in it. If not, a lamp will do, or just the memory of sun on your face. Close your eyes and feel the warmth. For these two minutes, nothing is being offered to you, and you don't need anything offered. Just the light, already here. When a want or a worry steps in front of it, notice the shade, and let it move aside. The bell holds the time.
Diogenes and the king. Offered anything by Alexander the Great, the Cynic asks him to stand out of his sunlight.
Your line: stand out of my light. Today, stand in the sun for one full minute. And when a want starts to block it, say the line, kindly. Day thirty-four.

screen: `DAY 34 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DIOGENES THROWS AWAY HIS CUP.`

howItsDone: The Cynics practiced radical simplicity, living with almost no possessions; many people today borrow a gentler version, cutting back on what they own and chase to make room for simple goods.

fork.setup: you're Diogenes, lying in the sun. Alexander the Great stands over you and says: ask me for anything you want. what do you ask?
options: that he stand out of your light.
fork.reveal: "stand out of my light." the king offered him the world, and what he wanted was the sun back.

original.note: Greek, kosmopolitēs: citizen of the world. Diogenes's answer when asked where he came from, and the root of English cosmopolitan.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rude old man and a funny comeback.
what it means: almost everything we chase blocks a simple good that's already shining on us.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 6.38 and Plutarch, Alexander 14; the tub was a pithos, a large clay storage jar (DL 6.23), and kosmopolitēs is DL 6.63.

sources.ref: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.38

notes: Date and place: Corinth, c. 336–335 BCE, when Alexander was about 20; DL 6.38 places Diogenes sunning himself in the Craneum. Confirm.
Crates as Diogenes's student: DL 6.85–87 says Crates was a pupil of Diogenes (some sources say of Bryson). Confirm.

'Stand out of my light' and 'if I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes' are paraphrased from DL 6.38 and Plutarch, Alexander 14 (no PD translation on the list); the fork reveal puts the famous phrase in quotation marks as the story's line. Confirm acceptable.
